summary: A 1970 note with comments on the Host/Host protocol document, by D. C. Walden. It is feedback on a draft of the host-to-host protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: Feedback on a draft of the rules for computers talking to each other.

subtitle: Comments on the early host-to-host protocol specification.

tldr.problem: The early host-to-host protocol has several design issues: marking wastes bits, links cannot be reused for different destinations, the allocation mechanism does not match receiver needs, and error control is insufficient.
tldr.mechanism: Walden proposes multiple changes: eliminate marking by sending leader and data as separate messages, limit global link count and add pseudo-links for local multiplexing, match allocations to receiver buffer sizes, and replace error codes with end-to-end acknowledgments.
tldr.outcome: These suggestions influenced the development of the protocol, though most required IMP program changes. Several ideas, particularly on pseudo-links and simplifying table lookups, addressed real complexity issues in the NCP design.

today: RFC 65 is Unknown status. Many of Walden's suggestions were discussed but required IMP changes, which constrained what could be adopted. However, his feedback influenced protocol discussions and the eventual TCP/IP design.

sections.title: Overview of Feedback
sections.content: Dave Walden from A/S Norsk Data-Elektronikk comments on the Host-Host Protocol document by S. Crocker. His comments address seven major areas of the specification, ranging from message format to connection management and error handling.
sections.plainLanguage: A network engineer reviews a draft and notes problems with how it is designed.

sections.title: Format and Connection Issues
sections.content:
On marking: Walden agrees with earlier proposals to eliminate marking. He suggests sending the leader and data as two consecutive messages instead, which simplifies processing. If the maximum message length is a multiple of all machine word sizes (such as 2880 × 2 bits), successive messages can be placed directly without any shifting.

On links: Walden observes that links have no value beyond identifying a connection, since there are 512 possible links per destination and thus do not significantly speed table lookups. He proposes limiting the global link count to a fixed number (32, 64, or 256) for all destinations, making link allocation simple. To recover the multiplexing benefit, he suggests adding a 'pseudo-link' field chosen by the sender and included in all non-control messages. This allows a single link to multiplex multiple logical connections, with the NCP using the link for receive table lookups and the pseudo-link for send table lookups.

On control messages: Walden argues control messages should use a dedicated control socket rather than a special control link, which removes a special case from the protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: The current design has links that try to do too much. Use fewer links, and let senders tag their messages with their own numbers instead.

sections.title: Allocation, Cease, and Error Handling
sections.content:
On allocation: Walden notes that the receiver wants allocations in units matching its buffer size, not in sender message units which may vary. This causes memory fragmentation problems.

On cease mechanism: Walden suggests the cease mechanism for flow control is overcomplicated. The sender can track ALLs and GVBs with a simple bit counter and ignore duplicate GVBs; there is no need for special irregular messages if the receiver is not told about cease status.

On resources: Walden encourages assigning sockets permanently to network resources and maintaining a directory of socket-to-resource mappings at each site.

On error control: Walden considers the ERR error code mechanism insufficient and complicated. He proposes replacing it with simple end-to-end acknowledgments from receiving process to sending process on every message. If an acknowledgment is not received in time, the sender retransmits. This single mechanism catches errors at any layer, whereas ERR only catches bugs from bugs in the primary mechanism.
sections.plainLanguage: Make allocations match how the receiver wants to organize memory. The flow-stop mechanism is too complex. And instead of special error codes, just have every message acknowledged, and the sender retries if no reply.
